title: Scarcity and economising
context: Analyze scarcity, economising, and who participates in economic decision-making. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Scarcity disappears once a household earns a steady salary because income removes all limits.
Economising means making careful use of limited resources rather than treating them as if they were unlimited.
Nobody can fully opt out of economic decisions, because even inaction is a choice about scarce time or money.
Only registered businesses face scarcity; households with regular income never need to economise on their spending.
Exchange requires that at least one party is an entrepreneur; households can never participate directly in exchange.
tactical_explanations:
A steady salary changes how a household budgets, but it does not erase scarcity. Food, rent, transport, and leisure still compete for the same euros after payday. Income rearranges limits; it does not abolish them. The claim that scarcity disappears once wages arrive is therefore wrong.

So the statement is False.

Economising is careful ranking of limited means against competing uses. Treating time, money, or materials as if they were unlimited is the opposite of that discipline. Households cut discretionary spending when cash is tight; firms delay purchases when stock is low. The statement names that careful use correctly, so it fits the chapter idea of economising.

So the statement is True.

Refusing to choose is still a choice about scarce means. Sitting out a purchase leaves money for later and frees time that could have been spent shopping or working. Even "doing nothing" allocates hours that cannot be reused. Households decide whether to save or spend; workers decide whether to take overtime; students decide whether to study or rest. In each case limited time and money force an allocation, including the allocation called inaction. Nobody steps outside that logic by opting out of markets or businesses. The statement is right that economic decisions follow people into everyday life, not only into registered firms.

So the statement is True.

Households with regular income still face rent, food, energy, and transport bills that compete for one budget. Scarcity is not reserved for registered businesses. A salaried family that skips a holiday to cover heating is economising in the same sense as a shop managing stock. Restricting scarcity to firms alone misreads who faces limited means.

So the statement is False.

Households buy bread, pay for repairs, and sell used goods without becoming entrepreneurs. Exchange is any agreed swap of goods or services, including ordinary consumer purchases. Requiring an entrepreneur on at least one side invents a rule the chapter does not use.

So the statement is False.

title: Goods, services, needs, and wants
context: Analyze the distinction between goods, services, needs, and wants. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Goods must be intangible; any tangible item automatically counts as a service instead.
Services are intangible activities performed for someone, such as installing software or preparing a drink.
Needs are things necessary for well-being, whereas wants are desired but not essential for basic well-being.
Both households and businesses have needs that may be fulfilled through exchange with other economic actors.
Scarcity means resources are limited, so individuals and businesses must economise rather than assume unlimited supply.
tactical_explanations:
Goods are tangible items such as bread, phones, or spare parts. Services are intangible activities such as repairs or tutoring. Calling every tangible item a service reverses the definitions. A loaf of bread remains a good even though it is physical.

So the statement is False.

Installing software, preparing a drink, or cutting hair are activities performed for someone, not physical objects handed over as stock. That intangibility is what makes them services. The café sells both roasted beans (a good) and barista labour (a service) side by side, which shows the split in one shop.

So the statement is True.

Needs cover what supports basic well-being: food, shelter, essential healthcare, reliable transport to work or school. Wants cover desired extras such as designer trainers, flavoured specialty drinks, or entertainment upgrades that life can continue without. The boundary can be fuzzy at the edges, yet the chapter still treats the distinction as useful. Craving a particular latte flavour is typically a want; securing calories and warmth is a need. Confusing the two labels muddles priorities when budgets are tight. The statement states the contrast cleanly and correctly.

So the statement is True.

Households need food and shelter; manufacturers need components and labour hours. Both sides meet those needs through buying and selling with other actors. Exchange is not reserved for one side of the market. Businesses purchase inputs just as families purchase groceries.

So the statement is True.

Scarcity means means are limited relative to uses. Individuals and firms therefore economise instead of assuming endless supply. Unlimited-stock thinking would erase the need to prioritise, which scarcity forbids.

So the statement is True.

title: Households, entrepreneurs, and everyday exchange
context: Analyze the roles of households and entrepreneurs in everyday exchange of goods and services. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Only consumers ever exchange goods; businesses are legally barred from all trade with households.
Only individual consumers have needs; registered businesses operate with zero internal needs of their own.
Choosing to keep pocket money unspent means a teenager has avoided making any economic decision.
Exchange is one way needs and wants get fulfilled when households and businesses trade with each other.
Because money is used, barter arrangements can never count as genuine exchange.
tactical_explanations:
Businesses sell to households every day: bakeries, cafés, repair shops, and online retailers. Trade between firms and consumers is ordinary exchange, not a legal prohibition. Claiming only consumers may trade invents a ban that does not exist.

So the statement is False.

Firms need raw materials, spare parts, energy, and staff time to keep operating. Those internal requirements are genuine needs, not consumer-only feelings. A bakery without flour cannot bake; a repair shop without screens cannot fix phones. Zero internal needs would describe an empty shell, not a working business.

So the statement is False.

Leaving pocket money unspent is itself an allocation of scarce cash and time. The teenager chooses saving over buying, which ranks one use of limited means above another. Economic decisions are not only purchases; holding money idle, delaying a trip, or skipping a market stall all rearrange scarce resources. Opting out of spending does not opt out of economics. The claim that unused pocket money means no decision was made confuses "no purchase" with "no choice."

So the statement is False.

When households buy goods or services from businesses, and when businesses buy inputs from suppliers, needs and wants get fulfilled through exchange. Direct swaps and money-mediated trades both count. Exchange is one practical channel for satisfying those pressures, not a side show.

So the statement is True.

Barter is exchange without money: lessons for a bookshelf, vegetables for childcare. Using cash is common but not required for a swap to count as genuine exchange. Money facilitates trade; it does not define it.

So the statement is False.

title: Business Operations and Institutional Needs
context: Consider households, startups, and manufacturing firms interacting in a market system. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Businesses provide goods like computers and services like installing software for people to satisfy their needs.
Manufacturers of smartphones may have an operational need for electronic components produced by specialised suppliers.
To fabricate components, a manufacturer requires raw materials and a workforce rather than operating in isolation.
Individuals frequently exchange goods and services directly and are fully active participants in trading.
Households need food, shelter, and medical care, and they also want leisure activities such as cinema visits.
tactical_explanations:
Computers are tangible goods; installing software is an intangible service. Businesses supply both so people can meet needs and wants. The statement pairs those examples correctly.

So the statement is True.

Smartphone makers depend on specialised electronic components from other firms. Without those inputs, assembly lines stop. That operational dependence is a business need satisfied through supplier exchange, not a consumer-only category.

So the statement is True.

Fabricating components requires raw materials, machines, and a workforce. No manufacturer runs in isolation from input markets. Labour hours, metals, plastics, and energy must be obtained and allocated. The claim that production needs materials and people rather than magic self-sufficiency matches how firms actually operate. Isolation would mean no supply chain and no output. The statement therefore describes ordinary manufacturing correctly.

So the statement is True.

Individuals buy groceries, pay for repairs, sell used goods, and hire tutors. They are not passive spectators waiting for firms to invent trade. Direct household participation in exchange is normal economic life, not an exception.

So the statement is True.

Food, shelter, and medical care are household needs; cinema visits are wants. Families pursue both through limited budgets. The statement separates those categories in a way that matches the chapter.

So the statement is True.

title: Corner café: beans and cappuccinos
context: Consider a corner café where customers buy bags of coffee beans and pay baristas to prepare drinks. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: The bag of roasted beans is a good and the barista's drink preparation is a service.
Needs and wants are identical concepts, so there is no meaningful difference between craving caffeine and a flavoured latte.
A habitual craving for a particular drink is more accurately a want if it is not essential for basic well-being.
Because the café is a business, it cannot itself be said to have needs such as reliable suppliers.
Paying for beans or drinks fulfils needs or wants through exchange on both sides of the transaction.
tactical_explanations:
Roasted beans in a bag are a tangible good. The barista preparing a drink performs an intangible service. One café transaction can include both categories at once, exactly as the statement says.

So the statement is True.

Needs support basic well-being; wants are desired extras. Craving caffeine for alertness and ordering a flavoured specialty latte are not identical ideas. Collapsing them into one concept erases the prioritisation households use when money is tight. The café setting makes the difference visible: fuel versus flourish.

So the statement is False.

A habitual craving for a particular branded drink usually sits in the want column if life continues without that exact flavour. Basic hydration and calories can come cheaper. Habit strength does not automatically promote a preference into a need. The chapter keeps needs tied to essential well-being, not to routine desire. Calling the specialty drink a want is the accurate label here, even for a daily customer who feels strongly about it.

So the statement is True.

Cafés need reliable bean suppliers, working machines, and staffed shifts. Those operational requirements are business needs. Being a registered firm does not erase them. Without suppliers, the corner café cannot sell drinks at all.

So the statement is False.

Customers pay; the café supplies beans or prepared drinks. Each side gets something it values through exchange. Needs or wants are fulfilled on both sides of that payment.

So the statement is True.

title: Jonas: bus pass or game skin
context: Consider jonas has twelve euros pocket money and must choose between an eight-euro bus pass and a ten-euro game skin. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: The bus pass is a need for getting to school, while the game skin is a want rather than a basic necessity.
Because both items have a price, they must both be classified as needs rather than wants.
Individuals face economic decisions about scarce resources even before they run a business or register as entrepreneurs.
Choosing to save the twelve euros and buy nothing means Jonas has opted out of all economic decision-making.
Once Jonas buys the bus pass, his want for the game skin permanently disappears and can never return.
tactical_explanations:
Twelve euros cannot cover both an eight-euro bus pass and a ten-euro game skin. Getting to school sits closer to a need; a cosmetic game skin is a want. Jonas's budget forces a ranking between them, and the labels in the statement match that ranking.

So the statement is True.

Price alone does not turn an item into a need. Many wants are priced; many needs are cheap. A ten-euro skin remains a want even though it costs money. Classification follows well-being, not the price tag.

So the statement is False.

Economic decisions begin whenever limited means meet competing uses, including pocket money before any business registration. Jonas chooses between transport and entertainment with a fixed twelve euros. Students, teenagers, and other individuals allocate scarce cash and time long before they become entrepreneurs. Restricting economics to registered firms would leave everyday budgets unexplained. The statement correctly places individuals inside economic decision-making from the start.

So the statement is True.

Saving the twelve euros and buying nothing is still a choice: hold cash now, forgo both the pass and the skin today. Inaction reallocates scarce money over time. Claiming that buying nothing opts Jonas out of economics confuses "no purchase" with "no decision."

So the statement is False.

Buying the bus pass uses current cash; the desire for the game skin can return next week when new money arrives. Wants are not permanently erased by one purchase. Preferences can recur after budgets refresh.

So the statement is False.

title: PhoneFix screen repairs
context: Consider phoneFix Wien replaces cracked screens using spare parts ordered in limited monthly batches. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Screen replacement is a service, while a phone case sold at the counter is a good.
Because PhoneFix is a business rather than a household, its monthly spare parts can never run scarce.
A customer buying a decorative case purely for its design is satisfying a want rather than a basic need.
Repairing a phone never fulfils a need because phones are luxury items outside normal economic analysis.
A limited monthly batch of parts forces the shop to economise by prioritising which jobs to accept.
tactical_explanations:
Replacing a cracked screen is labour performed for the customer, a service. A phone case sold at the counter is a tangible good. PhoneFix can offer both in one visit.

So the statement is True.

Spare parts arrive in limited monthly batches. Being a business does not create unlimited stock. When the batch runs down, further repairs wait. Scarcity of parts is exactly why the shop must prioritise jobs.

So the statement is False.

A decorative case bought for design rather than protection serves appearance and preference. That is a want, not a basic need for well-being. Functionally necessary repairs differ from optional styling accessories.

So the statement is True.

A working phone often supports work, school contact, and safety. Repairing it can restore a practical need, not merely a luxury whim. Excluding phones from economic analysis is artificial.

So the statement is False.

A fixed monthly parts batch cannot cover every cracked screen that walks in. PhoneFix must decide which jobs to accept, which to delay, and how to stretch inventory. That prioritisation is economising under scarcity. Unlimited-parts thinking would remove the need to choose; limited batches force ranking. The statement links the shop's constraint to careful allocation correctly.

So the statement is True.

title: Defining the economy from scratch
context: Consider during a first lesson students list core building blocks of economic life. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: The economy consists essentially of households and entrepreneurs interacting with one another.
Goods are tangible items, whereas services are intangible activities performed for someone.
Both households and businesses have needs, and exchange is one way those needs and wants get fulfilled.
Scarcity forces individuals and businesses to economise rather than assume unlimited resources.
Nobody, whether a household or a business, can truly opt out of making economic decisions.
tactical_explanations:
Households and entrepreneurs interacting through exchange form the core cast of everyday economic life. The statement names those building blocks without inventing extra actors as mandatory.

So the statement is True.

Goods are tangible items you can hold; services are intangible activities performed for someone. Bread versus delivery, beans versus barista work, tables versus assembly labour all illustrate the split. First-lesson definitions start there for a reason.

So the statement is True.

Families need food and shelter; firms need inputs and labour. Exchange is one channel that fulfils those pressures when parties trade. Needs and wants motivate both sides, and markets connect them. Listing households, businesses, needs, wants, and exchange together gives students a usable map of economic life rather than isolated vocabulary. The statement packs that map accurately.

So the statement is True.

Limited resources relative to uses is scarcity. Economising is the response: rank, cut, delay, or substitute. Assuming unlimited means would deny the problem economics studies. Individuals and businesses share that constraint.

So the statement is True.

Inaction, saving, spending, and producing are all allocations of scarce means. Neither households nor firms can step outside that logic permanently. Opting out of one market is still choosing how to use limited time and money.

So the statement is True.

title: Herr Novak's bakery
context: Consider herr Novak sells bread at his Linz bakery and charges one euro extra for doorstep delivery. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Herr Novak acts as an entrepreneur, while the families buying his bread act as households.
Bread is a good and doorstep delivery is a service, matching the distinction between tangible and intangible offerings.
Because Herr Novak owns a business, he personally has no needs of his own.
Paying for delivery is not exchange because a service has no monetary value once it has been performed.
Flour and oven fuel are unlimited for any bakery, so Herr Novak never has to economise on ingredients.
tactical_explanations:
Herr Novak runs the bakery as an entrepreneur; families buying bread act as households. Those roles meet at the counter when bread and money change hands.

So the statement is True.

Bread is a tangible good. Doorstep delivery is an activity performed for the customer, a service, often priced with an extra euro. Tangible versus intangible offerings sit side by side in one bakery order.

So the statement is True.

Owning a bakery does not cancel Herr Novak's personal needs for food, rest, housing, and income. Entrepreneurs remain people with household pressures even while they supply others. Business ownership and personal needs coexist. Claiming he has no needs of his own confuses the firm role with a person who somehow stops needing anything. The counterexample is ordinary life after closing time.

So the statement is False.

Paying one euro extra for delivery is exchange of money for a service. The service has value at the moment of agreement even though the activity is intangible and finishes when the loaf arrives. Denying monetary value after performance misunderstands how services are traded.

So the statement is False.

Flour and oven fuel are limited stocks that cost money and run down. Bakeries economise on ingredients constantly. Unlimited flour is a fiction, not bakery practice.

So the statement is False.

title: Exchange without money
context: Assess statements about exchange, barter, and fulfilling needs. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Two neighbours swapping gardening lessons for a handmade bookshelf still counts as exchange even without money.
Exchange can only occur when euro banknotes or electronic transfers are used between the parties.
Wood used to build the bookshelf is a limited resource, so the carpenter must economise on how much he uses.
Gardening lessons are a service because they are an activity performed for the neighbour, not a physical item.
Individuals, not only businesses, have needs and wants that direct exchange can help satisfy.
tactical_explanations:
Gardening lessons swapped for a handmade bookshelf is barter: each side gives something valued. Exchange does not require banknotes. Neighbours completing that swap still trade goods and services in the economic sense.

So the statement is True.

Euro cash and electronic transfers are common media, not the definition of exchange. Barter and in-kind swaps count whenever parties agree to trade. Requiring money would erase those trades from economics.

So the statement is False.

Wood for the bookshelf comes from limited timber. Using more on one project leaves less for the next commission or repair. The carpenter must decide thickness, waste, and offcuts carefully. That is economising under scarcity of materials. Treating wood as endless would ignore cost and availability. The statement ties limited wood to careful use correctly.

So the statement is True.

Gardening lessons are activities performed for the neighbour, not a physical object left behind like the bookshelf. That intangibility makes them a service. The swap therefore pairs a service with a good.

So the statement is True.

Individuals have needs and wants that direct neighbour-to-neighbour exchange can satisfy. Businesses are not the only actors with those motives. The gardening-for-bookshelf deal shows household-level trade working.

So the statement is True.

title: Petra's dining table commission
context: Consider petra pays carpenter Fabian 650 euros for an oak dining table he builds and delivers. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Petra's family acts as a household and Fabian acts as an entrepreneur in this transaction.
The finished dining table is a good because it is a tangible item Fabian produces and delivers.
Paying for the table fulfils the family's need for furniture through exchange.
Fabian has no genuine need for timber because raw materials are merely wants for any business.
Timber is a limited resource, so Fabian must economise on how much oak he uses per commission.
tactical_explanations:
Petra's family buys as a household; Fabian builds and sells as an entrepreneur. The 650-euro oak table deal places those roles on opposite sides of one exchange.

So the statement is True.

The finished dining table is a physical object Fabian produces and delivers. Tangibility puts it in the goods category, distinct from pure labour services such as advice without a delivered item.

So the statement is True.

Furniture for daily meals is a practical household need. Paying Fabian transfers money for the table and thereby fulfils that need through exchange. The family does not fabricate the oak piece itself; market trade supplies it. Exchange here is the channel linking carpenter output to household use. The statement describes that fulfilment accurately.

So the statement is True.

Timber is an essential input for Fabian's commissions. Without oak he cannot build the table. Calling raw materials mere wants for any business understates operational necessity. Inputs required to produce are needs of the firm.

So the statement is False.

Oak stock is limited per purchase and per forest supply. Fabian must economise on how much wood each commission consumes. Wasteful cuts raise cost and shrink what remains for the next job.

So the statement is True.

title: Needs, wants, and who has them
context: Analyze claims about needs, wants, and which actors in the economy face them. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: A manufacturer of laptops may need specialised electronic components from suppliers to keep production running.
High-tech manufacturers have zero internal needs because only end consumers ever experience genuine need.
Households buy goods and services from businesses to satisfy both needs and wants in daily life.
Wants disappear automatically once every need has been fully satisfied in a given month.
Teenagers with pocket money are outside the economy until they register a business or join a formal household.
tactical_explanations:
Laptop makers depend on specialised components from suppliers. Production stops without those parts. That dependence is a genuine manufacturing need met through exchange.

So the statement is True.

High-tech firms need chips, boards, energy, and skilled labour. End consumers are not the only actors who experience need. Zero internal needs would halt the plant. The claim invents a consumer-only monopoly on need.

So the statement is False.

Households buy groceries, transport, repairs, and entertainment from businesses. Some purchases cover needs; others cover wants. Daily life runs through those exchanges. The statement correctly places both categories on the household shopping list and names businesses as the counterpart. Without that channel, families would have to produce everything themselves.

So the statement is True.

Satisfying food and rent this month does not erase desires for leisure, upgrades, or gifts. Wants can persist or return after needs are covered. Automatic disappearance of wants once needs are met is wishful, not descriptive.

So the statement is False.

Teenagers with pocket money already allocate scarce cash and time. They participate as individuals in the household sphere long before registering a firm. Excluding them until formal registration misdraws the boundary of the economy.

So the statement is False.

title: Lukas end-of-month pocket money
context: Consider student Lukas has 300 euros monthly for transport, toiletries, and designer trainers. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Ninety euros for transport and toiletries covers needs, while 140-euro trainers cover a want.
Because Lukas receives money from parents, he is not part of the household side of the economy.
Buying trainers makes his need for transport disappear for the rest of the month.
Wanting trainers is irrational and therefore falls outside the scope of economics entirely.
A fixed monthly sum is an unlimited resource that never needs to be economised.
tactical_explanations:
Transport and toiletries support daily functioning; 140-euro designer trainers mainly express preference and style. With 300 euros monthly, Lukas covers needs first in the ninety-euro slice and a want in the trainers. The labels match the well-being split.

So the statement is True.

Money from parents still places Lukas inside a household budget. Receiving transfers does not eject him from the household side of the economy. Student allowances are ordinary household resource flows.

So the statement is False.

Buying trainers spends part of the month's cash; it does not cancel the ongoing need to get to class or work. Transport remains a separate claim on the budget. One want purchase cannot retire a recurring need. Confusing categories this way would leave Lukas stranded without a pass after the shopping trip. Needs and wants compete for money; they do not erase each other when one is bought.

So the statement is False.

Economics studies how people allocate scarce means among valued ends, including wants others might call frivolous. Irrationality is not a ticket out of the subject. Trainer preferences still face a limited 300-euro constraint.

So the statement is False.

A fixed monthly sum is limited by definition. Competing uses force economising. Calling 300 euros unlimited denies the scarcity Lukas actually faces before month-end.

So the statement is False.

title: Farmer Reinisch's market stall
context: Consider farmer Reinisch sells potatoes and carrots from eight hectares at a Saturday village market. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Reinisch acts as an entrepreneur at the stall while village buyers act as households.
Because farmland can theoretically be bought elsewhere, Reinisch's eight hectares should not be treated as scarce.
Potatoes and carrots are goods rather than services even though they must be cooked before eating.
Splitting eight hectares between crops is an economic decision Reinisch cannot avoid given limited land.
Paying cash at the stall is not genuine exchange because only barter counts as real economic trade.
tactical_explanations:
Reinisch sells produce as an entrepreneur at the stall; village buyers act as households. Market day pairs those roles over potatoes and carrots.

So the statement is True.

Eight hectares on this farm are limited land for this season's planting. The theoretical chance to buy other land elsewhere does not make today's hectares unlimited. Opportunity to expand later still leaves current acreage scarce relative to crop plans. Treating theoretical purchase options as proof of non-scarcity would erase almost every resource constraint. Reinisch must still split what he has now.

So the statement is False.

Potatoes and carrots are tangible products, hence goods, even if cooking comes later. Services would be activities such as delivery or catering. Raw vegetables remain goods on the stall.

So the statement is True.

Limited land forces crop choices: more potatoes mean fewer carrots on the same eight hectares. Reinisch cannot avoid that allocation. Economic decision-making is built into the field plan.

So the statement is True.

Cash payment for produce is money-mediated exchange, fully genuine. Barter is one form of trade, not the only valid one. Requiring barter alone would dismiss ordinary market stalls.

So the statement is False.

title: Market day in Hallstatt
context: Consider toni sells cheese wheels; Rosa offers children's face-painting; families buy for groceries or fun. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Toni and Rosa act as entrepreneurs while visiting families act as households.
A cheese wheel is a good and face-painting is a service.
Buying cheese for weekly groceries satisfies a need, while face-painting satisfies more of a want.
Paying for cheese or face-painting fulfils needs or wants through exchange on both sides.
Because Toni has only thirty wheels left, he must economise by allocating stock among queuing families.
tactical_explanations:
Toni and Rosa sell at the market as entrepreneurs; visiting families buy as households. Those roles structure the Hallstatt market day. That reading follows directly from the scarce means named in the statement, not from a different chapter topic.

So the statement is True.

A cheese wheel is a tangible good. Face-painting is an activity performed for a child, a service. One market can sell both categories from neighbouring stalls.

So the statement is True.

Cheese for weekly groceries supports nutrition and household provisioning, closer to a need. Face-painting is enjoyable decoration, closer to a want. Families may buy both, yet the motives differ when budgets tighten. The statement uses that contrast without claiming wants are worthless. Needs and wants can share one market trip while remaining distinct labels.

So the statement is True.

Paying for cheese or face-painting completes exchange: money for a good or service. Sellers receive revenue; buyers receive what they sought. Fulfilment of needs or wants runs through that two-sided trade.

So the statement is True.

Thirty wheels left cannot serve an endless queue. Toni must allocate remaining stock among families. That limited inventory forces economising on the spot.

So the statement is True.

title: Scarcity across actors
context: Assess whether scarcity and economising apply uniformly. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: A multinational corporation with large cash reserves still faces scarce managerial attention and factory capacity.
Households never economise because their wants are unlimited and budgets therefore do not constrain them.
Governments are excluded from scarcity because they can always raise taxes to fund any project immediately.
Economising is rational behaviour when a resource is limited relative to competing uses.
Entrepreneurs must economise on inputs such as labour hours and raw materials to stay viable.
tactical_explanations:
Large cash reserves do not create unlimited managerial attention or infinite factory capacity. Multinationals still rank projects and shift lines. Scarcity of attention and plant time survives big balance sheets.

So the statement is True.

Unlimited wants colliding with limited budgets is exactly why households economise. The claim reverses the logic: wants being many is a reason to prioritise, not a reason to ignore constraints.

So the statement is False.

Raising taxes takes political time, faces resistance, and still leaves this year's appropriated funds limited. Governments choose among roads, schools, and transfers under scarcity of current revenue and capacity. Immediate funding of every project is not available on demand. Excluding governments from scarcity misreads public budgeting. Councils and ministries economise too.

So the statement is False.

When a resource is limited relative to competing uses, ranking those uses is rational economising. Spending without priority would waste means that could serve higher-valued ends. The statement links limitation to careful allocation correctly.

So the statement is True.

Labour hours and raw materials cost money and run short. Entrepreneurs who ignore those limits lose viability. Economising on inputs is ordinary firm survival, not optional polish.

So the statement is True.

title: Elif: tutoring or unpaid internship
context: Consider elif can keep tutoring for 400 euros monthly or take an overlapping unpaid architecture internship. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Accepting the internship means opportunity cost is 400 euros monthly tutoring income forgone.
Because the internship pays nothing, choosing it has no opportunity cost at all.
Keeping tutoring means giving up career experience and prospects from the internship.
Opportunity cost must always be expressed only in euros with no other dimensions allowed.
Elif still allocates scarce time between tutoring and internship despite being a student.
tactical_explanations:
Taking the unpaid internship means Elif forgoes the 400 euros monthly she could earn tutoring. That forgone tutoring income is the opportunity cost of accepting the internship. Next-best paid alternative, not zero because the internship wage is zero.

So the statement is True.

Zero internship pay does not mean zero opportunity cost. The cost is what she gives up elsewhere, here tutoring income. Unpaid choices can be costly in forgone alternatives.

So the statement is False.

Keeping tutoring preserves cash but forgoes career experience and prospects the internship might open. Opportunity cost runs both ways: whichever path she picks, she loses the leading benefit of the other. Non-financial gains such as skills and networks count among those forgone benefits. The statement correctly names experience and prospects as what tutoring retains at the expense of the internship path.

So the statement is True.

Opportunity cost can be money, time, experience, health coverage, or other valued outcomes. Insisting on euros alone would shrink the concept. Elif's internship trade-off includes career dimensions that a pure euro rule would miss.

So the statement is False.

Student status does not remove scarce time. Elif still allocates hours between tutoring and internship. Individuals face allocation problems before they run firms.

So the statement is True.

title: Simon: car wash or volunteering
context: Consider simon can earn 45 euros at a car wash or volunteer at an animal shelter on the same Saturday. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: If Simon volunteers, the opportunity cost is the 45 euros forgone from the car wash shift.
Scarcity concerns only money, so Simon faces no real scarcity when choosing how to use his Saturday.
Personal satisfaction from volunteering cancels any opportunity cost that might otherwise exist.
Because Simon is a teenager, scarce-resource allocation concepts do not apply to his Saturday.
The shelter's dog food cost is part of Simon's opportunity cost when he chooses volunteering.
tactical_explanations:
Volunteering on Saturday means Simon does not take the car-wash shift. The 45 euros he would have earned is the leading forgone benefit, his opportunity cost.

So the statement is True.

Saturday hours are limited whether or not money is scarce that week. Choosing volunteering uses time that cannot also wash cars. Scarcity covers time and other means, not only cash balances.

So the statement is False.

One winery's shipment schedule to Germany is a firm-level logistics and sales plan. Crossing a border does not automatically make the unit macroeconomic. Micro still covers individual exporters.

So the statement is False.

Macro topics include growth, unemployment, inflation, interest rates, and aggregates such as trade totals. Export and import sums sit beside those headline variables as whole-economy measures. The ministry release belongs in that set. Listing trade totals with the classic macro list is accurate, not a stretch. That conclusion stays inside this statement's own nouns and does not borrow a different definition from another letter.

So the statement is True.

Economics seeks to explain why national export performance rises or falls over time using theories and evidence. That explanatory aim covers the ministry's aggregate series.

So the statement is True.

When the unit analysed is an individual firm's export choice, the work is microeconomics. Scope follows the decision maker, not the word export alone.

So the statement is True.

title: Confusing scope with topic
context: Consider students debate whether 'prices' and 'jobs' are always macro or micro topics. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Micro and macro study identical questions with no meaningful difference in scope.
Any discussion of wages is automatically macroeconomics because labour markets are national.
Economy-wide average wage growth published by a statistics office is macroeconomics.
A household choosing between two job offers compares micro-level alternatives under limited time.
Economics cannot explain individual choices, only nationwide aggregates.
tactical_explanations:
Micro and macro differ by scope: individual units versus the whole economy. Calling their questions identical erases that distinction students are meant to learn.

So the statement is False.

A single employer's wage offer or one worker's job choice is micro even though labour markets can also be studied nationally. "Wages" as a word does not force macro scope.

So the statement is False.

Economy-wide average wage growth from a statistics office is an aggregate series. That publication is macroeconomic analysis of labour-market outcomes for the nation. Contrast a household picking between two job offers, which stays micro. The same topic family, wages, splits by the unit measured. That conclusion stays inside this statement's own nouns and does not borrow a different definition from another letter.

So the statement is True.

Choosing between two job offers under limited time and attention is a household-level comparison. That is microeconomics even though wages are discussed.

So the statement is True.

Economics explains individual choices as well as nationwide aggregates. Micro exists for a reason. Restricting the science to aggregates alone is false.

So the statement is False.

title: Teacher's scope quiz
context: Consider a teacher lists examples and asks which are micro versus macro. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Micro examines individual households, businesses, or markets; macro examines the whole economy.
A single consumer choosing organic milk is microeconomics.
National unemployment rate is macroeconomics.
Economics explains and predicts at both scopes using theories about limited resources.
If an example mentions government, it must always be classified as macroeconomics.
tactical_explanations:
Micro examines individual households, businesses, or markets; macro examines the whole economy. That scope split is the standard branch definition.

So the statement is True.

One consumer choosing organic milk is a single-household purchase decision. Unit of analysis is micro regardless of how large the dairy industry is nationally.

So the statement is True.

The national unemployment rate summarises labour-market outcomes across the economy. That aggregate is a macroeconomic statistic used to track recessions and recoveries. It is not a story about one worker's Tuesday interview. Scope is national by construction in the rate itself. That conclusion stays inside this statement's own nouns and does not borrow a different definition from another letter.

So the statement is True.

Economics builds theories about limited resources at both micro and macro scopes and uses them to explain and predict. Branching does not abandon the scarce-means core.

So the statement is True.

Government appears in micro settings too, such as a firm bidding on a local contract. Mentioning government does not force a macro label by itself.

So the statement is False.

title: BrewPeak espresso price hike
context: Consider inês raises BrewPeak espresso prices after imported bean costs rise, thinking only about her Porto shop. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: National unemployment figures belong to microeconomics because each worker is an individual.
Macroeconomics is simply the study of any price change, including one café's espresso price.
Microeconomics never studies how two firms interact in one product market.
Macroeconomics refuses to discuss inflation because inflation starts in single shops.
Economics remains a science building theories to explain and predict behaviour despite imperfect human prediction.
tactical_explanations:
National unemployment figures are aggregates about the whole labour market. They belong to macroeconomics even though each worker is an individual person. Aggregation defines the scope.

So the statement is False.

Macroeconomics studies whole-economy variables, not every local price tweak. Inês raising espresso prices in one Porto shop is a micro pricing decision. Equating macro with any price change is a category error.

So the statement is False.

Microeconomics routinely studies how two firms interact in one product market: rivalry, pricing, entry, and customer switching. Denying that interaction work would empty industrial organisation and market analysis. BrewPeak competing with nearby cafés is exactly the kind of micro interaction the branch covers. The claim is false.

So the statement is False.

Inflation is a core macro topic: movements in the overall price level. Macro discusses inflation constantly; it does not refuse the subject because prices begin in shops. Aggregation from shops to the price level is the point.

So the statement is False.

Economics remains a science that builds theories to explain and predict behaviour even when human forecasts are imperfect. Imperfect prediction does not strip the subject of scientific aims.

So the statement is True.

title: Micro scope traps
context: Analyze traps students face when classifying examples as microeconomic rather than macroeconomic. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: A single farmer choosing between wheat and vegetable crops on limited irrigation water is microeconomics.
A single bakery setting its loaf price after flour costs rise is microeconomics.
A city bus company setting a new single-route fare is microeconomics when only that firm's pricing is analysed.
National GDP growth rate publication is macroeconomics because it summarises the entire economy.
Microeconomics can explain and predict behaviour of individual markets, households, and firms.
tactical_explanations:
Wheat versus vegetables on one farm, with irrigation water as the binding constraint, is a classic single-decision problem. Microeconomics studies how that farmer ranks crops and allocates scarce water, not national output totals.

So the statement is True.

After flour costs rise, the bakery resets its loaf price to protect margins. That pricing response sits inside one firm and one product market. Microeconomics is exactly the toolkit for firm-level cost shocks and the prices that follow, whereas GDP or the CPI would be the macroeconomic cousins of the same flour story.

So the statement is True.

A city bus operator changing a single-route fare, and analysts who look only at that firm's pricing, stay in micro territory. The object of study is one enterprise and one fare, not employment, inflation, or GDP for the whole city or country.

Even when many passengers ride that route, the scale of the crowd does not by itself flip the label to macroeconomics. What matters is whether the analysis aggregates the entire economy or stays with this carrier's price. Here the lens is narrow, so the micro label is the right one.

So the statement is True.

Publishing a national GDP growth rate summarises production across the whole economy. That is the signature of macroeconomics: economy-wide aggregates rather than one farm, bakery, or bus route. The same wheat or flour that appeared in micro examples can feed into GDP, but the publication itself is a macro statistic.

So the statement is True.

Explaining and predicting how households, firms, and individual markets behave is the ordinary job of microeconomics. The letter simply restates that scope without claiming anything about national aggregates.

So the statement is True.

title: Ride-hail surge pricing
context: Consider one ride-hail platform raises fares in one city district after a concert ends. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Studying surge pricing for one platform in one district is microeconomics.
Surge pricing is macroeconomics because many riders are affected at once.
If analysts measured whether district fare spikes raised the city's overall consumer price index, that index move would be macroeconomics.
Economics can predict how riders and drivers respond to a local price spike.
Individual market pricing never falls within economics because only governments set prices.
tactical_explanations:
Surge fares on one ride-hail platform in one district after a concert are a local price in a local market. Studying that spike is microeconomics, full stop.

So the statement is True.

Many riders feeling the surge at once does not turn the episode into macroeconomics. Macroeconomics tracks economy-wide aggregates such as the CPI, unemployment, or GDP. A crowded district market is still one market; crowd size is not the classifying rule.

If every busy shop were macro because many customers queued, the micro/macro split would collapse. The concert-driven fare spike stays micro unless the question shifts to city-wide price indexes.

So the statement is False.

Suppose analysts ask whether district fare spikes moved the city's overall consumer price index. The CPI is an economy-wide (or city-wide) average of prices, so that measurement question is macroeconomic even though the original surge began as a micro event.

The same concert can therefore support both labels depending on the object of study: platform pricing in one district is micro; whether those fares shift the index that summarises living costs across the city is macro. Scope follows the variable, not the concert itself.

So the statement is True.

Economics routinely models how riders cut trips, wait longer, or switch modes, and how drivers reposition when local fares jump. Prediction of those responses is part of ordinary price theory in a single market, which is squarely inside the discipline.

So the statement is True.

Governments are not the only price setters. Platforms, shops, and landlords set prices every day, and economics studies those markets. Claiming individual market pricing never falls within economics is simply wrong.

So the statement is False.

title: Competition authority case
context: Consider regulators investigate whether three mobile carriers colluded on text-message pricing nationally. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Investigating pricing across an entire national mobile market can involve macro-style market-wide analysis.
One subscriber choosing a cheaper text plan for her own phone is microeconomics.
Economics builds theories to explain firm behaviour and market outcomes including competition issues.
Microeconomics studies individual firm pricing strategies when one carrier alone is analysed.
Economics excludes market competition because only government budgets matter.
tactical_explanations:
A national probe into whether three mobile carriers colluded on text pricing looks across an entire industry market. That market-wide frame can borrow the language of broad, system-level analysis even though the product is still messaging rather than GDP. The letter's careful wording ("can involve macro-style market-wide analysis") fits that scale of inquiry.

So the statement is True.

A single subscriber switching to a cheaper text plan is a household-level choice inside one product market. That is ordinary microeconomics of consumer choice among plans.

The case also mentions a national collusion probe among operators, which is a different market-structure question. Treating the personal plan switch as if it answered the whole phone-market probe overreaches, so the letter does not stand as written.

So the statement is False.

Competition cases are standard territory for economic theory: how firms set prices, whether parallel pricing looks like collusion, and how market structure shapes outcomes. Building those explanations and predictions is what the discipline does.

Nothing in the mobile probe sits outside economics merely because regulators are involved. Firm behaviour and market outcomes, including competition issues, are core content rather than a side topic reserved for lawyers alone.

So the statement is True.

When the analyst isolates one carrier's pricing strategy on its own, the unit is a single firm. Microeconomics is the branch that studies that firm's incentives, costs, and prices without requiring a simultaneous model of national GDP.

So the statement is True.

Market competition is central to economics, not excluded from it. Government budgets matter in public finance, but they do not crowd firms, prices, and rivalry out of the subject. The absolute exclusion fails immediately.

So the statement is False.

title: Bookstore pricing experiment
context: Consider a regional bookstore chain tests a 5% price cut in one city branch and tracks only that branch's weekly revenue. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Analysing one branch's revenue after its own price change is microeconomics.
Central bank inflation targeting for an entire currency area is macroeconomics.
If the national statistics office later reported economy-wide consumer price inflation, that would be macroeconomics.
Micro focuses on individual households, businesses, and markets rather than the whole economy.
Economics tries to explain and predict outcomes such as how a branch responds to a price cut.
tactical_explanations:
Tracking one bookstore branch's weekly revenue after its own 5% price cut keeps the unit of analysis at a single outlet. That is microeconomics: one business, one price change, one revenue series.

So the statement is True.

Central-bank inflation targeting for an entire currency area aims at the general price level across many markets at once. That policy object is macroeconomic by construction, even though each shop's sticker price remains a micro fact on the shelf.

So the statement is True.

If the national statistics office later published economy-wide consumer price inflation, the series would summarise prices across the country, not the bookstore experiment alone. Economy-wide inflation is a macro aggregate.

The branch-level price cut can feed into that index as one tiny observation, yet the published inflation number itself answers a macro question: how the cost of living moved for the whole economy. Scope again follows the variable reported.

So the statement is True.

Microeconomics concentrates on individual households, businesses, and particular markets. It does not try to replace national accounts. The bookstore trial, a family's book budget, or a single city's book demand all sit on the micro side of that line.

So the statement is True.

Explaining and predicting how the branch's sales respond to the fare-style price cut is ordinary applied economics. The discipline exists to do that kind of outcome analysis.

So the statement is True.

title: Kelvinia rate rise
context: Consider kelvinia's central bank raises the key interest rate nationwide to slow inflation. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: GDP growth and one household's grocery list are analysed with identical tools and the same scope.
Interest rates on national policy are a micro topic because each loan is signed by one borrower.
Microeconomics covers only diagrams; macroeconomics covers only newspaper opinion.
Because mortgages of specific families change, the central-bank move is automatically microeconomics.
Economics tries to build theories explaining why central banks raise rates and predict inflation effects.
tactical_explanations:
GDP growth is an economy-wide production aggregate; one household's grocery list is a micro consumption plan. Analysts do not use identical tools and the same scope for both. National accounts, price indexes, and policy rates live in a different toolkit from a weekly shopping list.

So the statement is False.

A nationwide policy rate set by Kelvinia's central bank is a macro instrument even though each mortgage is signed by one borrower. The policy object is the whole credit market and inflation, not a single loan file.

So the statement is False.

Both branches use diagrams, data, and theories. Treating micro as "only diagrams" and macro as "only newspaper opinion" caricatures the split and is false.

So the statement is False.

Mortgage rates for specific families may change after the policy move, but that household consequence does not reclassify the central-bank decision as microeconomics. The bank raised the key rate nationwide to slow inflation, which is a classic macro policy action.

If every macro tool became micro whenever one family felt it, fiscal and monetary policy would lose their labels overnight. Transmission through household balance sheets is expected; the originating decision remains macro.

So the statement is False.

Economics builds theories of why central banks tighten when inflation runs hot and predicts how spending, investment, and prices may respond. Kelvinia's rate rise is exactly the sort of episode those theories are meant to organise.

So the statement is True.

title: Household savings rate national data
context: Consider central bank publishes average household savings rate across the entire country. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Average national household savings rate is a macroeconomic aggregate.
One family increasing its monthly savings by fifty euros is macroeconomics because saving is national policy topic.
Macro includes growth, unemployment, inflation, interest rates, and such economy-wide averages.
Economics explains and predicts how aggregate saving responds to interest rate changes.
Microeconomics studies one family's saving choice when that family alone is the unit analysed.
tactical_explanations:
An average household savings rate published for the entire country is an economy-wide aggregate. That places it firmly in macroeconomics. That reading follows directly from the scarce means named in the statement, not from a different chapter topic.

So the statement is True.

One family raising monthly saving by fifty euros is still a single household choice. Calling it macroeconomics just because "saving" also appears in national policy debates confuses the topic word with the unit of analysis.

National averages of saving are macro; this family's fifty euros are micro unless they are rolled into the published aggregate and studied as such.

So the statement is False.

Macroeconomics covers growth, unemployment, inflation, interest rates, and economy-wide averages such as the national savings rate. Those variables summarise many households and firms at once.

The central bank's publication of the average savings rate is one more member of that list. It does not claim that every private saving decision is itself a macro event; it reports the aggregate pattern across the country.

So the statement is True.

How aggregate saving shifts when interest rates change is a standard macro prediction problem. Economics supplies theories of that response and tests them against national data, which is exactly what the letter states.

So the statement is True.

When the analyst's unit is only one family's saving choice, microeconomics is the right branch. The same behaviour, averaged nationally, would be read as macro.

So the statement is True.

title: Startup funding round
context: Consider ten startups in a city receive venture funding; an analyst studies only one robotics firm's hiring plan. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Choosing a smartphone brand is classified as macroeconomics once the price exceeds €500.
Because venture capital is a national phenomenon, any firm-level study becomes macroeconomics.
Summing all startup investment in the country to assess economic growth would be macroeconomics.
Microeconomics explains and predicts behaviour of individual businesses and markets.
Economics excludes entrepreneurial firms because they are too small for scientific study.
tactical_explanations:
Smartphone brand choice is a household consumption decision regardless of whether the handset costs more than €500. Price level alone does not flip a micro choice into macroeconomics.

So the statement is False.

Venture capital may be discussed as a national trend, yet studying one robotics firm's hiring plan keeps the unit at a single enterprise. Firm-level studies remain microeconomics even when the funding source is a broader phenomenon.

So the statement is False.

Adding up all startup investment in the country to judge economic growth switches the lens to a national aggregate. That summation for growth assessment is macroeconomic work.

The analyst who stayed with one robotics hiring plan was doing micro; the statistician who totals investment across startups to speak about growth is doing macro. The same funding round can sit in either frame depending on whether the question is one firm's payroll or the country's capital formation.

So the statement is True.

Microeconomics explains and predicts how individual businesses and markets behave, including a single startup's hiring after a funding round. That is the branch's ordinary remit.

So the statement is True.

Small entrepreneurial firms are studied constantly in economics. Size does not exile them from scientific analysis; excluding them on that ground is false.

So the statement is False.

title: Budget airline seat sale
context: Consider a budget airline cuts base fares on one holiday route and tracks bookings for that route only. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Route-level fare and booking analysis for one airline is microeconomics.
Any airfare change is macroeconomics because airlines operate internationally.
Economics predicts how passengers on that route respond to the fare cut under limited budgets.
If the statistics office later reported national transport inflation, that would be macroeconomics.
Household holiday booking under a fare sale is micro consumption choice.
tactical_explanations:
Fare and booking data for one airline on one holiday route are a single-market, single-firm problem. Route-level analysis of that kind is microeconomics.

So the statement is True.

International networks do not automatically make every airfare change macroeconomic. A base-fare cut on one holiday route, tracked only for that route's bookings, remains a micro pricing experiment. Macro would enter if the question became national transport inflation or GDP.

So the statement is False.

Passengers on that route face limited holiday budgets. Economics predicts how many extra seats fill when the base fare falls, how early they book, and whether they switch from other modes. Those responses are textbook demand behaviour under scarcity of money and time.

The airline's own booking tracker for the route is collecting exactly the micro evidence such predictions need.

So the statement is True.

A later national transport inflation release from the statistics office would summarise prices across the transport category for the whole country. That index movement is macroeconomic even if one holiday route contributed a little to it.

So the statement is True.

A household booking a holiday seat under the sale is choosing consumption under a price change. That is micro consumption choice, not a national accounts exercise.

So the statement is True.

title: Tax-funded lighthouse
context: A coastal town funds a lighthouse through general taxation rather than individual tolls. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Money's store-of-value function is strengthened when inflation is very high and unpredictable.
Free riders would benefit from the beam without paying if funding relied purely on voluntary donations.
Tax financing can overcome free-rider problems by compelling contributions from beneficiaries broadly.
Because ships are private businesses, lighthouse services cannot be public goods by definition.
Public goods must always be provided free with zero cost to any taxpayer.
tactical_explanations:
Very high, unpredictable inflation destroys money's reliability as a store of value: cash held today buys much less tomorrow. The store-of-value function is weakened, not strengthened, under those conditions. The lighthouse story does not change that monetary fact.

So the statement is False.

If the beam were funded only by voluntary donations, ships could still navigate by the light without paying. That non-paying use is the free-rider problem the letter names.

So the statement is True.

Compulsory tax contributions pull funding from a broad base of beneficiaries and residents, so the lighthouse need not rely on voluntary gifts that free riders would skip. Tax finance is a standard way to overcome that underprovision risk for non-excludable services.

The coastal town's choice of general taxation rather than individual tolls fits that logic: the beam protects many vessels at once, and excluding non-payers from seeing the light is impractical.

So the statement is True.

Public-good status hinges on non-excludability and non-rivalry of the service, not on whether the ships that benefit are private businesses. A lighthouse beam can still be a public good while private vessels use it. The "private ships" argument does not redefine the good.

So the statement is False.

Public goods are often tax-financed; taxpayers do bear a cost. "Free at the point of use" is not the same as "zero cost to any taxpayer." The absolute claim fails.

So the statement is False.

title: Saving euros under low inflation
context: A worker holds 1,000 euros in a current account while inflation runs slightly below 2%. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Money still stores value but slowly loses some purchasing power under positive inflation.
Slightly below 2% inflation means purchasing power rises every year for cash holders.
Store-of-value function is weaker when inflation is positive even if moderate.
ECB target near 2% contrasts with destabilising very high inflation rates.
Purchasing power of held cash depends on general price level changes domestically.
tactical_explanations:
With inflation a little under 2%, the worker's €1,000 still works as a store of value from month to month, yet each euro buys slightly less over the year. Both parts of the letter hold.

So the statement is True.

Positive inflation, even slightly below 2%, means the price level is rising and cash holders lose purchasing power slowly. Purchasing power does not rise every year for idle cash; that would require falling prices (deflation), not mild inflation.

So the statement is False.

Any sustained rise in the general price level chips away at what a given cash balance can buy later. Moderate inflation still weakens the store-of-value function compared with stable prices, even when the erosion is slow enough that people keep using money day to day.

The worker's current account illustrates the point: the nominal balance can stay €1,000 while its real command over goods drifts down.

So the statement is True.

An ECB-style target near 2% aims at low, stable inflation, which is a different world from destabilising very high inflation that scrambles contracts and saving. The contrast in the letter is economically sound.

So the statement is True.

What the held cash can buy depends on domestic price-level changes for the goods the worker actually faces. That is the definition of purchasing-power risk for money balances.

So the statement is True.

title: Circular flow basics
context: Analyze the circular flow of income and spending: Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Stored cash never loses purchasing power because nominal euro amounts stay unchanged on the note.
A banknote's face value freezes its real purchasing power for decades.
Households can only appear on the spending side and never supply labour or capital to firms.
The circular flow shows how income earned from production returns as spending on output.
Government, banks, and foreign trade never appear in any circular-flow diagram.
tactical_explanations:
A note can keep the same printed face value while prices rise around it. Nominal euros unchanged on the paper do not protect real purchasing power; inflation still erodes what the cash buys.

So the statement is False.

Face value is a nominal label. Over decades of rising prices, the same banknote buys fewer goods. Real purchasing power is not frozen by printing a number on the note.

So the statement is False.

In the circular flow, households supply labour and capital to firms and earn income, then spend on goods. They are not trapped forever on the spending side only.

So the statement is False.

The circular flow of income and spending traces a loop: firms pay households for productive inputs, households use that income to buy output, and revenue returns to firms. Income earned from production thus comes back as spending on output.

That loop is the basic accounting story of how production, income, and expenditure hang together in a monetary economy, before adding banks, government, or trade in richer diagrams.

So the statement is True.

Extended circular-flow diagrams routinely include government, financial institutions, and foreign trade. Claiming they never appear is false.

So the statement is False.

title: Hyperinflation pocket money
context: In a country with very rapid price rises, a child's 20-euro note buys far less candy monthly. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Very rapid inflation sharply erodes purchasing power of nominally unchanged cash amounts.
Paying with a mobile transfer is exchange using money as medium of exchange.
Store-of-value function of money fails when inflation outpaces ability to spend or invest quickly.
ECB's slightly-below-2% target aims at stability far from such hyperinflation scenarios.
Purchasing power erosion under inflation affects households as well as firms holding cash.
tactical_explanations:
When prices race upward each month, a child's unchanging 20-euro note buys far less candy. Rapid inflation erodes purchasing power of nominally fixed cash.

So the statement is True.

A mobile transfer that settles a purchase uses money as the medium of exchange: value moves without bartering candy for something else. Digital payment still counts as monetary exchange.

So the statement is True.

Store of value requires that money held today still buy a useful bundle tomorrow. When inflation outruns the chance to spend or invest, cash melts in real terms and that function fails in practice.

The candy example is extreme but clear: waiting a few months with the same note leaves the child able to buy much less. Hyperinflation is precisely when store-of-value collapses for everyday balances.

So the statement is True.

An ECB target slightly below 2% is a stability goal meant to keep money reliable, far from the hyperinflation setting where monthly prices explode. The letter's contrast is correct.

So the statement is True.

Households and firms that hold cash both lose real purchasing power when inflation runs hot. The erosion is not limited to one side of the circular flow.

So the statement is True.

title: National park entry debate
context: Policals debate funding a national park via general tax versus gate fees only. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Clean air and preserved landscape benefits may extend beyond paying visitors, suggesting public-good elements.
Pure gate fees may exclude low-income residents while still leaving non-visitors benefiting from ecosystem services.
Tax funding can address free-rider issues when many benefit without direct payment.
National parks are never public goods because trees are physical objects you can touch.
Free-rider problems occur only in foreign trade and never in domestic environmental policy.
tactical_explanations:
Clean air and a preserved landscape often benefit people who never buy a gate ticket. Those spillover benefits are public-good elements sitting alongside any private visit experience inside the park.

So the statement is True.

Gate fees alone can price out low-income residents while ecosystem services still reach non-visitors. Both equity and free-rider tensions show up in that funding design.

So the statement is True.

When many residents benefit from conservation without paying at the gate, voluntary or fee-only finance underprovides relative to social benefit. Tax funding can collect from a broad base and ease that free-rider gap.

The political debate between general tax and gate fees is therefore not only about fairness at the entrance; it is also about whether non-excludable benefits get financed at all.

So the statement is True.

Touching trees does not decide public-good status. What matters is whether exclusion is hard and whether one person's enjoyment of the landscape crowds out another's. Physicality of trees is irrelevant to that test.

So the statement is False.

Free-rider problems appear constantly in domestic environmental policy, from clean air to open parks. They are not confined to foreign trade.

So the statement is False.

title: Money's three functions
context: Analyze the three functions of money in a modern economy: Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: High, erratic inflation makes cash a safer long-term store of value.
Inflation means any one product got dearer in a single aisle.
Street lighting never faces free riders because neighbours always chip in voluntarily.
Because money stores value, its purchasing power never changes over time.
Barter requires a double coincidence of wants, which money helps overcome as medium of exchange.
tactical_explanations:
High, erratic inflation makes cash a worse long-term store of value, not a safer one. Uncertainty about tomorrow's prices is exactly what undermines storing wealth in money.

So the statement is False.

Inflation refers to a general rise in the price level, not to one product getting dearer in a single aisle. A lone shelf-price hike can happen with stable overall inflation.

So the statement is False.

Neighbours do not always chip in for street lighting. Non-payers still enjoy the lit street, so free-rider incentives are real; voluntary funding often falls short.

So the statement is False.

Money can serve as a store of value in a low-inflation setting, yet its purchasing power still changes whenever the price level moves. "Never changes" is an absolute that inflation and deflation both refute.

Holding cash through a year of rising prices leaves the holder able to buy less even though the notes look the same.

So the statement is False.

Barter needs a double coincidence of wants: each party must want what the other offers at the same time. Money as medium of exchange breaks that requirement by letting sellers accept a common means of payment and buy what they want later.

So the statement is True.

title: Circular flow with government
context: Evaluate government's role in an extended circular flow: Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Government collects taxes from households and firms and spends on public services and transfers.
Government spending and taxation appear in extended circular-flow models linking public sector to private actors.
Households never receive anything from government, so no return flow exists in the circular model.
Subsidies and transfers are channels through which government redistributes income in the flow.
The circular flow shows only barter with no role for money as medium of exchange.
tactical_explanations:
Government taxes households and firms, then spends on public services and transfer payments. That two-way fiscal link is exactly what the letter states.

So the statement is True.

Extended circular-flow models add the public sector: tax withdrawals from private actors and government spending that returns purchasing power as services, wages, or transfers. Those links are standard once the simple household-firm loop is enriched.

So the statement is True.

Households receive public services, wages from public jobs, and transfers. Claiming they never receive anything from government, so no return flow exists, is false.

So the statement is False.

Subsidies to producers and transfers to households are the channels through which government redistributes income inside the circular flow. They do not have to be pure public goods to matter for the accounting loop.

A housing benefit or a firm subsidy both move purchasing power under public rules and show up in richer flow diagrams alongside taxes and public purchases.

So the statement is True.

Even the basic circular flow is usually drawn with money as the medium linking income and spending. It is not a pure barter diagram with no monetary role. The letter's denial is wrong.

So the statement is False.

title: Call centre task split

So the statement is False.

title: Input Costs and Supply
context: Analyze how changes in production costs shift the supply curve. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: When energy costs surge, equilibrium price may rise if demand remains unchanged.
Higher wages paid to warehouse staff can shift supply leftward for distribution services.
Cheaper imported components can shift supply rightward and lower equilibrium price.
Input cost changes move producers along the supply curve without shifting it.
A drop in steel prices shifts demand leftward because buyers expect weaker furniture.
tactical_explanations:
Surging energy costs shift supply leftward; with demand unchanged, equilibrium price tends to rise and quantity falls. Costlier production shows up in higher market prices.

So the statement is True.

Higher warehouse wages raise distribution costs, so firms offer fewer services at each old price: supply shifts leftward. Labour is an input whose price moves the supply curve.

A rightward supply move typically lowers equilibrium price when demand is unchanged; a leftward move does the opposite. Quantity adjusts at the new intersection.

Input relief and productivity gains are the practical reasons supply can expand without anyone changing the product’s sticker price first.

Cost, technology, capacity, or seller numbers change how much firms offer at each price in Input Costs and Supply. Those events shift supply rather than merely changing the good’s own price.

So the statement is True.

Cheaper imported components cut marginal cost, shifting supply rightward and typically lowering equilibrium price when demand holds. Input relief expands offers at each price.

At the intersection used in Input Costs and Supply, quantity demanded equals quantity supplied, so neither surplus nor shortage keeps forcing price to move.

Away from that point, one side of the market is frustrated and bids price back. Competitive adjustment is the path from imbalance toward balance.

So the statement is True.

Input cost changes shift the supply curve; they do not merely slide producers along an unchanged curve. Movement along supply is reserved for the product’s own price, holding cost shifters fixed.

So the statement is False.

Cheaper steel shifts furniture supply rightward by lowering costs; it does not shift demand leftward because buyers expect weaker furniture. Demand is about willingness to buy, not about input bargains for producers.

The because-clause overreaches. Even if one fragment sounds familiar, the causal link or always/never stretch does not hold.

Put the actors back in the correct category and the statement collapses without needing a new chapter of theory.

A concrete counterexample from Input Costs and Supply is enough: the absolute wording fails as soon as an ordinary case sits on the other side.

Compared with neighbouring letters in Input Costs and Supply, this one turns on drop, steel, prices rather than on a generic system slogan.

So the statement is False.

title: Technology and Productivity
context: Review how technological improvements shift supply by lowering production costs. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Technological progress that cuts unit cost shifts supply rightward, not leftward.
Improved irrigation technology may shift supply rightward for orchard fruit at each market price.
Automated sorting equipment can shift supply rightward for parcel delivery services.
Technology changes are supply shifters distinct from movements caused by the good's own price.
Rightward supply shifts from technology raise equilibrium price when demand is unchanged.
tactical_explanations:
